mainTopic: Which foods and measures are valid for an עירוב: majority practice versus individual measures, raw foods, the meaning of מזון, vowed-off loaves, and wine for a נזיר.
overview: The amud opens by finishing אביי's proof: in the laws of טומאה, the measure that suits rich people's clothing does not set the rule for the poor, so one group's custom (like the Persians' roasted meat) does not set the rule for עירוב. The גמרא rejects a suggestion to be strict in עירוב anyway, because רבי שמעון בן אלעזר measures an עירוב leniently for the sick, the old and the glutton. It then contrasts that ruling with his view that עוג מלך הבשן needs a doorway as big as himself, and explains that there the body simply has no other way out. Next come rulings that raw meat and raw eggs are valid for an עירוב, with a dispute over whether one egg or two is needed. The גמרא discusses the משנה about vowing off מזון, and רב הונא saves רב and שמואל by separating 'anything that nourishes' (זן) from real מזון. A long discussion follows about a loaf someone swore not to eat versus a loaf he forbade with 'עלי'. It ends with two traditions of רבי אליעזר's view. Finally, the גמרא shows that our משנה, which allows wine for a נזיר's עירוב, follows בית הלל. בית הלל's argument against בית שמאי continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Rich people's clothing is not measured by the poor
steps.stepSummary: The end of אביי's proof from טומאה of cloth: the larger measure that suits rich people's clothing does not set the rule for the poor, for whom smaller pieces still count.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the clothing of the rich does not set the measure for the poor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proof for אביי that started on the previous amud. The larger cloth size used for rich people's clothing does not set the rule for poor people, for whom smaller pieces still matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For טומאה, rich people's cloth counts only at a larger size (three by three טפחים), but poor people save even small scraps. The rich group's standard does not decide the law for the poor. אביי uses this to show that one group's special custom does not set the rule for everyone, just as the Persians' habit of eating roasted meat as a meal does not set the rule for עירוב.

phrases.english: But the clothing of the rich, for the poor — no.
phrases.notes: The final clause of a ברייתא about cloth sizes for טומאה, quoted as support for אביי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes אביי's proof, which began on the previous amud.
steps.raayaObject: אביי's rule that a minority custom (the Persians) is cancelled against the practice of most people.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on cloth measures for טומאה: the measure suited to the rich does not determine the law for the poor.

steps.title: Challenge: an עירוב can be measured by the individual
steps.stepSummary: One might say both rulings are simply stringent. But רבי שמעון בן אלעזר lets a sick or old person's עירוב be measured by his own small appetite, which is a leniency based on the individual.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say: here we are strict and there we are strict. But a ברייתא teaches that רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: we make an עירוב for a sick person or an old person with the amount of food that is enough for him. And for a glutton, we use an average meal of an ordinary person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a possible pushback: in טומאה the law is strict for the poor, so perhaps in עירוב we should also be strict and require the Persians' larger amount. It then attacks that suggestion with a ברייתא showing that עירוב measures lean toward leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If עירוב were ruled strictly, a sick person would need the normal amount and a glutton would need his own larger amount. Yet רבי שמעון בן אלעזר goes lenient both ways: the sick or old person uses his own smaller amount, and the glutton needs only an average meal. So עירוב is not ruled strictly, and there is no reason to require the Persians' larger amount.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you will say (introduces a possible defense)
but wasn't it taught in a ברייתא?
enough food for him (his own amount)
a glutton, someone who eats a lot

steps.confusionAlert: Both clauses are leniencies. The sick or old person may use less food, and the glutton does not need his own larger amount. Together they show that עירוב is not ruled strictly.

phrases.english: And if you say:
here it is a stringency and there it is a stringency,
phrases.notes: In טומאה the law is strict for the poor, so perhaps in עירוב too we should be strict and require the Persians' larger amount.

phrases.english: but wasn't it taught in a ברייתא,
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
We make an eiruv for a sick person or an elderly person with enough food for him.
phrases.notes: His own smaller amount for two meals.

phrases.aramaic: וּלְרַעַבְתָן, בִּסְעוּדָה בֵּינוֹנִית שֶׁל כׇּל אָדָם.
phrases.english: And for a glutton, with an average meal of an ordinary person.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָכָא לְחוּמְרָא וְהָכָא לְחוּמְרָא, וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a reading of אביי's comparison as 'both stringent,' then challenges that reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that עירוב, like the טומאה case for the poor, should be ruled strictly, which would require the Persians' larger amount.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר is lenient both ways: a sick or old person uses his own smaller amount, and a glutton needs only an average meal. So עירוב leans toward leniency, not stringency.

steps.title: The challenge stands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא admits that the challenge is not answered.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits it has no answer to the challenge from רבי שמעון בן אלעזר and moves on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'קשיא' marks that the 'be strict in both areas' suggestion cannot stand against this ברייתא. Since עירוב leans toward leniency, it need not follow the Persians' larger amount. The difficulty is against the suggestion, not against אביי.

keyTerms.meaning: it is difficult (the question stays unresolved)

steps.confusionAlert: 'קשיא' is weaker than 'תיובתא.' A 'קשיא' leaves a problem standing, but it does not formally refute the view.

phrases.english: It is difficult.
phrases.notes: The challenge is left unanswered.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge from step 2 without a resolution.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The suggestion to be strict in עירוב (following the Persians) does not stand against רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's lenient measures.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר seems to contradict himself about עוג
steps.stepSummary: For a glutton, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר uses the average person. But for עוג מלך הבשן, he requires a doorway as big as the giant himself, so there he measures by the individual.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי שמעון בן אלעזר really say this? But a ברייתא teaches that רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: for עוג מלך הבשן, his doorway must be as big as his full size!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions רבי שמעון בן אלעזר himself. It shows another ruling of his that seems to clash with the glutton rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the glutton, an unusual person is measured by the average. With עוג, an unusual person is measured by his own huge size. That looks like a contradiction: does the law follow the average person or the actual person?

keyTerms.meaning: and did he really say? (introduces a contradiction)
עוג, king of the בשן, the famous giant
as large as his full size

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main question for the whole section: when does the law use a general standard, and when does it go by the specific person?

phrases.aramaic: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר הָכִי?
phrases.english: And did Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar really say this?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Og, king of the Bashan —
phrases.notes: Refers to the laws of טומאת אוהל: which doorway of a house with a dead body counts as the way the body will leave.

phrases.english: his doorway must be as big as his full size!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר הָכִי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from attacking אביי to finding an internal contradiction in רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, whose ברייתא was just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's glutton rule, which uses an average meal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the case of עוג, the same תנא measures by the individual's actual size rather than the average, which seems inconsistent.

steps.title: עוג is different: there is no other way to get him out
steps.stepSummary: How does אביי, who follows the majority practice, explain the עוג ruling? With a giant there is no choice: the body cannot be cut into pieces, so only a doorway he fits through can be used.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אביי? There, what should one do? Should we cut him into pieces and take him out?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how אביי explains the עוג case, and answers that the giant's case is forced by reality, not by a general rule about individuals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the עוג case, the body physically has to leave through a doorway it fits through, and cutting it up is unthinkable. So the measure follows his size only because there is no choice. In עירוב there is no such practical limit, so the general practice of people can still set the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: should we cut him into pieces?

steps.whatToRemember: אביי: a minority custom does not set the measure for עירוב. The עוג ruling is an exception forced by physical reality, not a rule that each person is measured by himself.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches a key distinction: the law goes by an individual's size when reality forces it, but by general practice when a standard measure is possible.

phrases.english: And Abaye? (How does he explain this?)
phrases.notes: A short question: how does אביי handle the עוג ruling?

phrases.english: There, what should one do?
Should we cut him into pieces and take him out?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question: obviously not, so the doorway must fit him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers how אביי's majority-practice rule fits with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's עוג ruling from step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): physical necessity versus a choosable standard.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The עוג ruling shows that halachic measures generally follow the specific individual, which would undercut אביי.
steps.terutzMaskana: עוג is measured by his own size only because there is no other way to remove the body. Where a general standard is possible, as in עירוב, it follows common practice.

steps.title: Do the Sages disagree with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the חכמים argue with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's view that עוג's doorway is measured by his own size.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: Do the חכמים disagree with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question: does anyone argue with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר about measuring עוג's doorway by his size? This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר said a giant like עוג needs a doorway as big as he is. Now the גמרא wants to know whether this is a universal view or whether the חכמים hold differently.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (an open question)

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
Do the Sages disagree with

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר, אוֹ לָא?
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the עוג ruling from steps 4-5 and asks whether the חכמים disagree with it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the חכמים argue with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's rule that a giant's doorway is measured by his own size.

steps.title: Proof from רבי יוחנן: עוג's doorway is four טפחים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says even עוג's doorway is four טפחים, which suggests the חכמים use a fixed measure and disagree with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: עוג מלך הבשן — his doorway is four טפחים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof that the חכמים disagree: רבי יוחנן said that for עוג, a doorway of four טפחים is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is about טומאת אוהל: when a dead body is in a house, an opening of four טפחים marks the exit the body will be carried through, and that keeps the other openings pure. If even for עוג four טפחים is enough, then the measure is fixed and not based on his huge body, which goes against רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: עוג, king of the בשן, a famous giant

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the עירוב topic. This doorway law is about טומאת מת (a dead body in a house), and the גמרא brings it only to see whether a fixed measure or a personal measure is used.

phrases.english: Come and hear,
for Rabba bar bar Chana said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Og, king of Bashan —
his doorway is four handbreadths.
phrases.notes: Four handbreadths is the standard size for the opening that saves the others from impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an answer to the question of step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That the חכמים disagree with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר and use a fixed measure even for a giant.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן, quoted by רבה בר בר חנה: עוג's doorway is four טפחים.

steps.title: Rejection: the four-handbreadth opening is the obvious exit
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off: רבי יוחנן's case is a house with many small openings and only one of four טפחים, which is obviously the one that will be widened.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is a case where there are many small openings and only one that is four טפחים. Surely, when they widen an opening to take him out, that is the one they will widen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by explaining that רבי יוחנן was talking about a special situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן did not mean that four טפחים is big enough for עוג. He meant that among many tiny openings, the single four-טפח one is the one people will widen to remove the body, so only that one becomes impure. This tells us nothing about whether the חכמים disagree with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.whatToRemember: The question of whether the חכמים disagree with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר is left without proof. רבי יוחנן's ruling is about which opening will be used, not about the size a giant needs.

phrases.english: There, it is where there are many small openings,
and there is one that is four handbreadths,
so certainly, when one widens an opening —
it is that one he widens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from רבי יוחנן is fully neutralized. It cannot show that the חכמים disagree.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof misreads the case. Four טפחים matters because it is the only opening large enough to be widened, not because it is the right size for עוג.

steps.title: An עירוב may be made with raw meat or raw eggs
steps.stepSummary: רב says an עירוב may be made with raw meat, and רב שימי בר חייא adds raw eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר רב אשי said in the name of רב: One may make an עירוב with raw meat. רב שימי בר חייא said: One may make an עירוב with raw eggs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the laws of עירוב and gives two rulings: raw meat and raw eggs are both acceptable for an עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב must be made with food. Raw meat and raw eggs are not usually eaten as they are, but some people do eat them when needed. That is enough for them to count as food for an עירוב.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Ashi said that Rav said:
One may make an eruv with raw meat.
Rav Shimi bar Chiyya said:
One may make an eruv with raw eggs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. After the side discussion about עוג, the גמרא goes back to which foods are valid for an עירוב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw meat and raw eggs are valid foods for an עירוב.

steps.title: How many eggs are needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how many raw eggs are needed for an עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how many eggs are needed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question about the egg ruling: what amount is required? This sets up the answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב needs enough food for two meals. Since eggs come in whole units, the גמרא wants to know how many eggs equal that amount.

phrases.english: And how many?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the required quantity in רב שימי בר חייא's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The number of raw eggs needed for a valid עירוב.

steps.title: One egg or two
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says one egg is enough. סיני (רב יוסף) says two are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: one. סיני said: two.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question and disagree: one egg or two eggs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree that raw eggs work. They argue only about how many eggs make up the required two-meal amount. סיני is a nickname for רב יוסף, given because of his broad knowledge of sources.

keyTerms.meaning: סיני, a nickname for רב יוסף

steps.confusionAlert: סיני here is a person (רב יוסף), not Mount Sinai.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
One.
Sinai said: Two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the quantity question from step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A dispute: רב נחמן בר יצחק says one egg, and סיני (רב יוסף) says two eggs.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: one who vows off food may drink water
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: someone who vows not to eat מזון may still have water and salt.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: One who vows off מזון is permitted water and salt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from our משנה to set up an inference and a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה teaches that water and salt are not counted as מזון for vows. This line is the base text the גמרא will now analyze.

phrases.english: One who vows off nourishment
is permitted water, etc.
phrases.notes: The full משנה says water and salt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Water and salt do not count as מזון regarding a vow.

steps.title: Does the משנה refute רב and שמואל?
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה it seems that every food except water and salt is called מזון. That seems to contradict רב and שמואל, who say בורא מיני מזונות is said only on the five grains.
steps.simpleTranslation: Only salt and water are not called מזון; everything else is called מזון. Shall we say this refutes רב and שמואל? For רב and שמואל both said: One says בורא מיני מזונות only on the five grains.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads an inference from the משנה and asks whether it refutes רב and שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה implies that every food besides water and salt counts as מזון. But רב and שמואל limit the word מזונות in the ברכה to the five grains. If all foods are מזון, why should only grains get the ברכה of מזונות?

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this is a refutation?
The blessing 'Who creates kinds of nourishment'
The five grains (wheat, barley, spelt, rye, oats)

steps.whyThisMatters: This connects the definition of מזון in vows and עירוב to the practical הלכה of which foods get the ברכה of בורא מיני מזונות.

phrases.aramaic: מֶלַח וּמַיִם הוּא דְּלָא אִיקְּרִי מָזוֹן,
phrases.english: It is only salt and water that are not called nourishment,
but all other things are called nourishment.
Shall we say this is a refutation
of Rav and Shmuel?
For Rav and Shmuel both said:
One does not recite 'Who creates kinds of nourishment'
except over the five species of grain alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the משנה quoted in step 12 and uses it to challenge רב and שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב and שמואל's rule that בורא מיני מזונות is said only on the five grains.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the משנה treats every food except water and salt as מזון, then the term מזונות should not be limited to grain foods.

steps.title: Why bring a second challenge?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why it bothered to challenge רב and שמואל again, since they were already refuted once before.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't we already refute them one time?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask a side question about the challenge in Step 13. Why attack רב and שמואל again if they were already refuted? This sets up the short answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The view of רב and שמואל (that בורא מיני מזונות is said only on the five grains) was already refuted from another source elsewhere in the תלמוד. So bringing another challenge looks unnecessary. The גמרא wants to explain why it is doing this.

keyTerms.meaning: we refuted him / we challenged him

phrases.english: But didn't we already refute him one time?
phrases.notes: Refers to an earlier refutation of רב and שמואל

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side question about why the challenge in Step 13 is needed at all
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why raise a new refutation against רב and שמואל when one already exists

steps.title: Here is one more refutation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that it is simply adding another refutation from this source as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say there is a refutation of them from here too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that yes, they were already refuted. It is just pointing out one more source that also refutes them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge from the משנה about מזון is not meant to replace the earlier refutation. It is an extra proof against רב and שמואל. This leaves the challenge open, so the next step can try to answer it.

phrases.english: Let us say there is a refutation of them from this as well!
phrases.notes: An extra refutation, not a replacement

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: This is an additional refutation, brought alongside the earlier one

steps.title: The vow was about anything that nourishes
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא explains that the משנה is about someone who vowed off 'anything that nourishes' (כל הזן), which is wider than the word מזון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: The case is where he said, 'Anything that nourishes is forbidden to me.' Only water and salt don't nourish, but everything else does.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא defends רב and שמואל against the challenge in Step 13. He says the person in the משנה did not use the word מזון. He used the wider phrase 'anything that nourishes.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'anything that nourishes' (כל הזן) covers almost every food. Only water and salt are left out. But the specific word מזון, as used in the ברכה of בורא מיני מזונות, can still mean only the five grains. So the משנה no longer contradicts רב and שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: (is forbidden) upon me, a vow phrase

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up זן (anything that nourishes, which is very wide) with מזון (filling, sustaining food, the five grains). רב הונא's whole answer depends on these being two different words.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The case is where he says, 'Anything that nourishes is forbidden to me.'
It is water and salt that do not nourish,
but all other things do nourish.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּאוֹמֵר כׇּל הַזָּן עָלַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13 against רב and שמואל
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's vow used the word מזון, so מזון would include all foods except water and salt
steps.terutzMaskana: The vow was 'כל הזן', a wider term. מזון itself can still mean only the five grains

steps.title: רבי יוחנן ate huge amounts of fruit and said he had not eaten anything nourishing
steps.stepSummary: A story about רבי יוחנן eating enormous amounts of fruit from גינוסר, then swearing he hadn't tasted anything 'nourishing,' suggests that fruit does not count as זן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: When we followed רבי יוחנן to eat the fruits of גינוסר, if we were 100 people, each person took 10 fruits. If we were 10 people, each took 100. Every 100 of these fruits could not fit into a three-סאה basket. רבי יוחנן ate them all and said: I swear I have not tasted anything nourishing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's claim that everything except water and salt 'nourishes.' It brings a story where רבי יוחנן ate a huge amount of fruit and still said he had not tasted anything nourishing (זיונא).
steps.deeperAnalysis: If fruit counts as 'nourishing,' how could רבי יוחנן swear he had not eaten anything nourishing after eating so much fruit? This suggests that the term זן does not include fruit. That would break רב הונא's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: the fruits of גינוסר, very fine fruits from near the כנרת

phrases.english: But didn't Rabba bar bar Ḥana say:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה אָזֵילְנָא בָּתְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
phrases.english: When I would go after Rabbi Yoḥanan
to eat the fruits of Genosar,
when we were a group of a hundred —

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה מְנַקְּטִינַן לְכׇל חַד וְחַד עַשְׂרָה עַשְׂרָה.
phrases.english: each and every one of us would take ten.
When we were a group of ten —

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה מְנַקְּטִינַן לְכׇל חַד וְחַד מְאָה מְאָה.
phrases.english: each and every one of us would take a hundred.

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל מְאָה מִינַּיְיהוּ (לָא) הֲוֵי מַחֲזִיק לְהוּ
phrases.english: And every hundred of them could (not) be held
phrases.notes: The bracketed לא is a textual variant. Either way, the fruits were very large

phrases.english: by a basket of three se'ah,
and he would eat all of them,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: שְׁבוּעָתָא דְּלָא טְעִים לִי זִיּוּנָא!
phrases.english: and say: I swear that I have not tasted anything nourishing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's answer in Step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's claim that everything except water and salt is called זן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן ate a lot of fruit and still swore he had eaten nothing 'nourishing.' So fruit is apparently not זן.

steps.title: He really said מזונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the wording of רבי יוחנן's statement: he said he had not tasted מזונא, meaning real filling food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say: 'מזונא' (filling food).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by correcting the words of the story. רבי יוחנן said he had not eaten מזונא, real filling food. He did not say he had eaten nothing nourishing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the corrected wording, the story supports the idea that fruit is not מזון, which fits רב and שמואל. But fruit can still count as זן, nourishing. So רב הונא's answer stands.
steps.whatToRemember: זן (nourishing) covers every food except water and salt. מזון (filling food) means only the five grains. This difference saves רב and שמואל from the challenge in Step 13.

phrases.english: Say: 'sustaining food.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 17
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the quoted story
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן said 'זיונא,' meaning fruit is not nourishing at all
steps.terutzMaskana: He said 'מזונא.' Fruit is not מזון, but it still counts as זן

steps.title: A loaf you swore not to eat versus a loaf you forbade on yourself
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא in the name of רב rules that a loaf someone swore not to eat may be used for his עירוב, but a loaf he forbade on himself ('this loaf is upon me') may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said in the name of רב: If he said 'I swear I will not eat this loaf,' we may make an עירוב for him with it. If he said 'This loaf is forbidden to me,' we may not make an עירוב for him with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about using food for an עירוב. It compares two ways of vowing off a loaf of bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a שבועה, the person only forbids himself from eating. The loaf itself is not forbidden, and an עירוב does not need to be food this person can eat, so it may be used. Saying 'this loaf is upon me' forbids the loaf itself to him, including any benefit from it. Using it for an עירוב is a benefit, so it may not be used.

keyTerms.meaning: an oath, where the person binds himself

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the wording of a vow matters. Binding yourself (שבועה) is different from forbidding the object itself (כיכר זו עלי). That difference decides whether the food can still serve as an עירוב.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said that Rav said:
'I swear that I will not eat this loaf' —
we may make an eiruv for him with it.
'This loaf is forbidden to me' —
we may not make an eiruv for him with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל כִּכָּר זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new teaching about vows and עירוב food, linked to the earlier vow discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A loaf forbidden by שבועה may be used for an עירוב. A loaf forbidden as 'כיכר זו עלי' may not.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to allow an עירוב even with a loaf forbidden by 'עלי'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא saying one may make an עירוב with a loaf a person vowed off. It suggests this means even when he said 'עלי', which contradicts רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: 'Someone who vows off a loaf, we may make an עירוב for him with it.' Doesn't that mean he said 'it is forbidden to me' (עלי)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to argue with רב הונא's ruling from Step 19.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא uses the general word נודר (vows) and does not mention an oath. The simple reading is a normal vow, 'this loaf is עלי.' If so, the ברייתא allows an עירוב in exactly the case where רב הונא forbade it.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (from a ברייתא or משנה)
We may make an עירוב (with it)
Is it not that...? (proposing a reading in order to attack)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
phrases.notes: Standard formula for challenging an אמורא from a tannaitic source.

phrases.english: One who vows off a loaf —
we may make an eruv for him with it.
Is it not where he said 'it is forbidden to me'?
phrases.notes: This is the case רב הונא forbade.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's ruling in Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that a loaf forbidden with 'עלי' cannot be used for an עירוב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא allows an עירוב with a vowed loaf, and the plain meaning of a 'vow' is 'עלי'.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about an oath on 'this' loaf
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא means a case where he swore not to eat 'this' loaf, not a case of 'עלי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is where he said '[I swear I won't eat] this [loaf].'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב הונא by reading the ברייתא as speaking about an oath (שבועה).
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath forbids the person from eating. It does not make the loaf itself forbidden. So the loaf can still serve as his עירוב, which fits רב הונא's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: This one (shorthand for an oath about 'this loaf')

phrases.english: No, it is where he said 'this' [loaf].
phrases.notes: Meaning: 'I swear that I will not eat this loaf.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-defining the case in the source (אוקימתא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was assumed to be about a vow of 'עלי'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about an oath, where the loaf itself is not forbidden, so it agrees with רב הונא.

steps.title: The ברייתא's own wording supports reading it as an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that the ברייתא itself goes on to say the rule applies only when he said 'I swear I will not taste it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It also makes sense this way, because the later part teaches: 'When is this? When he said: I swear that I will not taste it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for its answer from the next line of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא limits its own ruling with 'אימתי' (when?) and names the case: an oath. This shows the ברייתא never allowed an עירוב with an 'עלי' loaf, just as רב הונא said.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is reasonable (introducing support)
The later part of the source
When? (a phrase that limits a rule)

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable,
for it teaches in the latter clause:
When [does this apply]? When he said:
'An oath that I will not taste it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer given in Step 21.
steps.raayaObject: The reading that the ברייתא is about an oath.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's own limiting clause: 'אימתי, בזמן שאמר שבועה שלא אטעמנה'.

steps.title: So with 'עלי', is the עירוב not allowed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא would say about 'עלי' and assumes the answer is that an עירוב is not allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said 'עלי', what? Is it then true that we may not make an עירוב for him with it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next challenge. It spells out what the ברייתא must mean in the 'עלי' case if רב הונא is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא allows an עירוב only with an oath, then with 'עלי' the עירוב must be forbidden. The גמרא states this clearly so it can test it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Upon me' (a vow that makes the item forbidden to me)
So too / is it indeed so?

phrases.english: But if he said 'it is forbidden to me,' what?

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי דְּאֵין מְעָרְבִין לוֹ בָּהּ?
phrases.english: Is it indeed that we may not make an eruv for him with it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out what Step 22's reading implies, as a setup for the challenge in Step 24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the ruling is for a loaf forbidden with 'עלי' according to this reading of the ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Assumed: an עירוב may not be made with it, which leads directly into the next challenge.

steps.title: Then the ברייתא should have drawn the line inside the case of a regular loaf
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that if 'עלי' forbade the עירוב, the ברייתא should have taught that contrast directly instead of moving to the case of a loaf of הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, instead of teaching 'this loaf is הקדש — we may not make an עירוב with it, because we don't make an עירוב with הקדש,' it should have divided its own case and taught: 'When is this said? When he said this [loaf, with an oath]. But if he said עלי, we may not make an עירוב for him with it!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading again. The ברייתא's choice of example suggests it saw no difference between an oath and 'עלי'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's next forbidden case is a loaf made הקדש, a completely new topic. If 'עלי' were also forbidden, the easier and closer contrast would have been inside the same case: oath is allowed, 'עלי' is not. Since it skipped that contrast, it seems even 'עלי' is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Consecrated property belonging to the בית המקדש
Let it make a distinction and teach within the same case
In what case are these words said?

phrases.english: If so,
instead of teaching 'this loaf is consecrated'
we may not make an eruv for him with it,
because we do not make an eruv with consecrated items —
let it distinguish and teach within the same case:
In what case is this said? Where he said 'this' [with an oath],
but if he said 'it is forbidden to me' —
we may not make an eruv for him with it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the conclusion stated in Step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the ברייתא forbids an עירוב with an 'עלי' loaf, which supports רב הונא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא would normally teach the closest contrast. Jumping to הקדש instead of contrasting oath with 'עלי' suggests 'עלי' is also allowed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This uses a common גמרא tool: asking why a source picked one example over a closer one (ליפלוג וליתני בדידה).

steps.title: רב הונא could reply that the other reading has a problem with the first clause
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא replies that if 'עלי' were always allowed, the earlier clause limiting the rule to an oath would make no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא can say to you: Rather, what do you want? That wherever he said 'עלי' we may make an עירוב? Then the first clause is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב הונא by turning the question back on the challenger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The clause 'אימתי, בזמן שאמר שבועה' clearly limits the permission to an oath. If 'עלי' were allowed too, that limit would be pointless. Since both readings face a difficulty, the ברייתא is no proof against רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you (defending an opinion)
Rather, what would you say? (turning the question back)
The earlier clause of the source

steps.confusionAlert: The same clause ('אימתי... שבועה') was called the סיפא in Step 22 and is called the רישא here. It is the later line compared to the opening rule, but the earlier line compared to the הקדש case. It is the same line.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא's counter-question shows that the 'אימתי... שבועה' clause does not fit easily with permitting 'עלי'. This is not the final word: the next step rereads the ברייתא as permitting 'עלי' too, and step 27 says the difficulty against רב הונא remains.

phrases.english: Rav Huna could say to you:
Rather, what [would you say]?
That wherever he said 'it is forbidden to me' we may make an eruv?
Then the first clause is difficult!
phrases.notes: The clause 'When? When he said: an oath that I will not taste it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַב הוּנָא: אֶלָּא מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 24 on behalf of רב הונא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-difficulty: the other reading clashes with the ברייתא's own limiting clause.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because the ברייתא skipped the oath vs. 'עלי' contrast, 'עלי' must also be allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: For now, רב הונא deflects the challenge: the reading that 'עלי' is always allowed clashes with the 'אימתי' clause. The next step reinterprets that clause by filling in missing words.

steps.title: The ברייתא is missing words: even 'עלי' counts like an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the ברייתא has missing words. Read in full, it teaches that we may make an עירוב with a loaf the person vowed off, even if he said 'עלי', because that counts like saying 'I swear I will not taste it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Words are missing from the ברייתא, and this is what it means: if someone vows off a loaf, we may make an עירוב for him with it. Even if he said 'This loaf is forbidden to me', it counts as if he said 'I swear I will not taste it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the problem raised in the last step by saying the ברייתא is missing some words. It fills in the missing words so the ברייתא reads smoothly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 25 showed that the clause 'only if he said I swear' cannot sit well with the idea that 'עלי' is always fine. The fix is that the ברייתא really means 'even עלי works, because עלי is treated like a שבועה.' So the loaf only becomes forbidden to him as food. It can still serve as his עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: Something is missing from the text; we must fill in words
'Upon me': the wording of a נדר that forbids the object to oneself
An oath; it binds the person, not the object
We may make an עירוב (set up the עירוב food)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think חסורי מיחסרא means the ברייתא is 'wrong.' The גמרא is only saying the text is written briefly, and the full meaning includes extra words.

phrases.english: Words are missing,
and this is what it teaches:
One who vows off a loaf,
we may make an eruv for him with it,
and even if he said "upon me" —
phrases.notes: i.e., 'this loaf is forbidden to me'

phrases.english: it is as though he said:
"I swear that I will not taste it."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the textual problem from step 25 by adding missing words to the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to limit the rule to a שבועה, leaving 'עלי' unclear.
steps.terutzMaskana: The full ברייתא says even 'עלי' is treated like a שבועה, so an עירוב is allowed.

steps.title: This reading still contradicts רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the newly filled-in ברייתא allows an עירוב even with 'עלי', and that still contradicts רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Either way, this is a difficulty for רב הונא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notes that the fix in step 26 solved the wording problem but created a problem for רב הונא. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא holds that when someone says 'עלי', we may not use that loaf for his עירוב. The full ברייתא now openly says the opposite: even 'עלי' is fine. So רב הונא's view seems to go against a ברייתא.

phrases.english: In any case, it is difficult for Rav Huna!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the reading from step 26 into a challenge against רב הונא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that 'עלי' prevents making an עירוב with the loaf
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The completed ברייתא explicitly permits an עירוב even with 'עלי', which directly contradicts רב הונא.

steps.title: רב הונא follows רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב הונא based his ruling on the opinion of רבי אליעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He (רב הונא) said his view following רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב הונא by saying he holds like a different תנא, רבי אליעזר. The next step will bring the source for this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא does not have to agree with every ברייתא. If a תנא backs him, he may follow that תנא's view. So the ברייתא in step 26 reflects one view, and רב הונא follows another.

keyTerms.meaning: He said it in line with (a certain authority)
A תנא whose view is cited as support

phrases.english: He stated it in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the Amora's view to a dissenting תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא seems to go against the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב הונא follows רבי אליעזר, who disagrees with that ברייתא.

steps.title: A ברייתא where רבי אליעזר splits oath and 'עלי'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא in which רבי אליעזר rules that with a שבועה we may make the עירוב, but with 'עלי' we may not, just like רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי אליעזר says that if someone says 'I swear I will not eat this loaf,' we may make an עירוב for him with it. If he says 'This loaf is forbidden to me,' we may not make an עירוב for him with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source proving that רבי אליעזר holds like רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שבועה forbids the person from eating, but the loaf itself stays a normal loaf, so it can still be his עירוב. 'עלי' puts the ban on the loaf itself, so in this version רבי אליעזר does not allow it as an עירוב. That is exactly רב הונא's position.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Eliezer says:
"I swear I will not eat this loaf" —
we may make an eruv for him with it.
"This loaf is upon me" —
phrases.notes: i.e., forbidden to me

phrases.english: we may not make an eruv for him with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the claim in step 28.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אליעזר distinguishes between a שבועה and 'עלי', as רב הונא does

steps.title: Another ברייתא has רבי אליעזר allow 'עלי'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this by quoting a different ברייתא. There רבי אליעזר allows an עירוב with 'עלי' and forbids it only with הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי אליעזר really say that? But a ברייתא teaches: this is the rule. If a person forbids himself from a food, we may make an עירוב for him with it. If a food is forbidden to a person, we may not make an עירוב for him with it. רבי אליעזר says: 'This loaf is forbidden to me' — we may make an עירוב for him with it. 'This loaf is הקדש' — we may not make an עירוב for him with it, because we do not make an עירוב with הקדש items.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether רבי אליעזר really said this. It quotes another ברייתא where he says the opposite about 'עלי'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this ברייתא, the first opinion splits 'person forbids himself' (a שבועה) from 'food is forbidden' (עלי). רבי אליעזר disagrees and puts 'עלי' on the permitted side. For him, only הקדש blocks the עירוב. That contradicts the ברייתא from step 29 and pulls away רב הונא's support.

keyTerms.meaning: But was it not taught (in a ברייתא)?
Forbids himself (the ban is on the person)
Food that becomes forbidden (the ban is on the object)
Property dedicated to the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: In this ברייתא, the view that splits שבועה from 'עלי' belongs to the first (anonymous) opinion, not to רבי אליעזר. רבי אליעזר's own split is between 'עלי' and הקדש.

phrases.english: And did Rabbi Eliezer say this?
But it was taught: This is the rule:
A person who forbids himself from a food —
phrases.notes: e.g., an oath

phrases.english: we may make an eruv for him with it.
Food that is forbidden to a person —
phrases.notes: e.g., 'this loaf is upon me'

phrases.english: we may not make an eruv for him with it.
Rabbi Eliezer says:
"This loaf is upon me" — we may make an eruv for him with it.
"This loaf is consecrated" —
we may not make an eruv for him with it,
because we do not make an eruv for him with consecrated items!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר הָכִי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא brought in step 29 as רבי אליעזר's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי אליעזר forbids an עירוב with 'עלי'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second ברייתא has רבי אליעזר explicitly allowing 'עלי' and forbidding only הקדש, the opposite of step 29.

steps.title: Two תנאים report רבי אליעזר differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that two תנאים disagree about what רבי אליעזר held.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are two תנאים, and they disagree about what רבי אליעזר's opinion was.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clash between the two ברייתות. It says each one comes from a different תנא reporting רבי אליעזר's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two ברייתות give opposite versions of רבי אליעזר's view, so the גמרא concludes that later תנאים disagreed about what he said. רב הונא follows the version in step 29. That version is still a valid tradition, so רב הונא keeps his support.

keyTerms.meaning: According to; in the view of

steps.whatToRemember: A שבועה forbids the person and still allows the loaf as an עירוב. הקדש always blocks it. 'עלי' is disputed: one version of רבי אליעזר (followed by רב הונא) forbids it, while another version permits it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common גמרא tool. When two ברייתות quote the same תנא in opposite ways, the גמרא solves it by saying later תנאים disagreed about his view.

phrases.english: Two Tannaim
disagreeing about the view of Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute among later תנאים about an earlier תנא's view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות contradict each other about רבי אליעזר, which seems to remove רב הונא's support.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each ברייתא is a different tradition about רבי אליעזר, and רב הונא follows one of them.

steps.title: The משנה follows בית הלל, not בית שמאי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that an עירוב may be made for a נזיר with wine. It states that this משנה does not follow the view of בית שמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'We may make an עירוב for a נזיר with wine, etc.' Our משנה is not like בית שמאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It immediately says that this line does not match the opinion of בית שמאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נזיר may not drink wine, yet the משנה lets wine count as his עירוב food. The גמרא notes that someone holds otherwise, namely בית שמאי. It will prove this in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: We may make an עירוב (set down food to establish a שבת 'home base')
A person who took a vow not to drink wine, among other restrictions
Etc.: the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: 'We may make an eruv for a nazir with wine, etc.'
phrases.notes: Quotation of the משנה that opens the new discussion.

phrases.english: Our Mishnah is not like Beit Shammai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic after the discussion of רבי אליעזר and רב הונא concluded.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's permission to use wine for a נזיר's עירוב follows בית הלל and does not follow בית שמאי.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows the disagreement between בית שמאי and בית הלל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא. בית שמאי forbid making an עירוב for a נזיר with wine or for a ישראל with תרומה. בית הלל allow both.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: בית שמאי say we may not make an עירוב for a נזיר with wine, or for a ישראל with תרומה. בית הלל say we may make an עירוב for a נזיר with wine and for a ישראל with תרומה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves its last statement by quoting a ברייתא. In it, בית שמאי say no to both cases and בית הלל say yes to both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית שמאי seem to require that the עירוב food be fit for the person himself to eat. בית הלל are satisfied if the food is fit for someone else. So our משנה, which allows it, matches בית הלל.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught (in a ברייתא)
The portion of produce given to a כהן, which a non-כהן may not eat
A regular Jew who is not a כהן

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'ישראל' means a non-כהן, not 'any Jew'. That is why he cannot eat תרומה.

phrases.english: As it was taught: Beit Shammai say:
We may not make an eruv for a nazir with wine
or for a (non-kohen) Israelite with terumah.
Beit Hillel say:
We may make an eruv for a nazir with wine
and for an Israelite with terumah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source behind the claim in step 32 that the משנה does not follow בית שמאי.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that our משנה does not follow בית שמאי
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recording that בית שמאי forbid while בית הלל permit an עירוב with wine for a נזיר and תרומה for a ישראל

steps.title: בית הלל begin to argue against בית שמאי
steps.stepSummary: בית הלל start a challenge to בית שמאי with the words 'Don't you agree...'. The rest of the argument continues in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית הלל said to בית שמאי: 'Don't you agree...'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. בית הלל are about to remind בית שמאי of a case they already agree to, so they can use it against them in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Don't you agree' is a classic way to argue from something the other side already accepts. בית הלל will point to a case where בית שמאי admit the food need not be fit for the person himself. The actual case appears on the next amud.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית הִלֵּל לְבֵית שַׁמַּאי:
phrases.english: Beit Hillel said to Beit Shammai:
Don't you agree...
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית הִלֵּל לְבֵית שַׁמַּאי: אִי אַתֶּם מוֹדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Inside the ברייתא, בית הלל begin to argue for their view against בית שמאי.
steps.kashyaTarget: בית שמאי's view that one may not make an עירוב with food the person himself cannot eat
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An argument from concession: בית הלל will point to a case בית שמאי already accept, showing the same logic should allow wine for a נזיר and תרומה for a ישראל.
